conceptTag: Price your product during a shortage
readerTitle: Half the butter, twice the line: running a bakery through a shortage
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (동네 베이커리, 4단계 결정) + 실제 연구 (Kahneman·Knetsch·Thaler 1986 공정성 설문). 베이커리 수치는 모두 설명용
insight: 공급 부족 때의 결정은 가격 하나가 아니라 가격, 재료 배분, 고객 배분, 부족이 끝난 뒤의 약속이 이어진 묶음이다.
misconception: 공급이 부족하면 가격을 그대로 두는 것이 공정하고, 수요가 넘치면 최대한 올리는 것이 이득이다.

sources.text: Kahneman, D., Knetsch, J. L., & Thaler, R. (1986). Fairness as a Constraint on Profit Seeking: Entitlements in the Market. American Economic Review, 76(4), 728–741.
베이커리 사례와 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 눈 삽 문항: 폭설 다음 날 철물점이 삽 가격을 $15에서 $20로 올린 것에 대해 응답자 82%가 불공정하다고 답함(n=107). 원문 표의 수치를 게시 전에 다시 확인하세요.
같은 연구에서 비용 상승을 가격에 반영하는 인상은 대체로 공정하다고 받아들여졌다는 결론. 카드에는 일반적 서술로만 적었습니다.
공급 부족 시 가격 인상 규제(price gouging 법)는 국가·지역마다 다릅니다. 법률 조언이 되지 않도록 7번 카드에서 '지역 규칙을 확인하라'는 수준으로만 언급했습니다.

cards.title: Half the butter, twice the line.
body: You run a neighborhood bakery famous for its croissants. You sell 300 a day at $4.
On Monday your supplier calls. A dairy shortage means you'll get half your usual butter for about six weeks, and it will cost 40% more. Four decisions are coming. Make each one before you read on.

image.label: Bakery counter with a half-empty butter crate and a long line outside
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 동네 빵집 카운터 위에 반쯤 빈 버터 상자, 창밖으로 길게 늘어선 줄. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What happens to the croissant price?
body: Butter in each croissant used to cost $0.50. Now it costs $0.70. You'll bake only 150 a day, and they'll sell out by 9 a.m. whatever you charge.

options.text: Keep it at $4. Raising prices in a shortage feels wrong
options.feedback: Customers stay happy, but you absorb the cost rise on fewer sales. The line, not the price, decides who gets a croissant, and people pay in waiting time.

options.text: Raise it to $4.25, with a sign explaining butter costs and saying it's temporary
options.feedback: You cover the higher cost and tell people why. Most customers accept a raise that passes on a real cost they can see.

options.text: Raise it to $7. They'll sell out anyway
options.feedback: You'd earn more this month. But regulars read it as cashing in on a crisis, and they remember long after the butter returns.

cards.title: People judge *why* a price went up.
body: In a 1986 survey, economists Daniel Kahneman, Jack Knetsch and Richard Thaler asked people about a hardware store that raised snow shovel prices from $15 to $20 the morning after a snowstorm. **82%** called it unfair.
Yet most people accepted price rises that passed on higher costs. Same higher price, different reason, different verdict.
Your $0.25 raise tracks your own cost. That's why the sign matters: it shows the reason.

image.label: Handwritten bakery window sign explaining a temporary price rise
image.brief: 빵집 창문에 붙은 손글씨 안내문: "Butter costs are up. Croissants $4.25 until supply returns." 따뜻한 톤, 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Where should the scarce butter go?
body: Say you chose B. Now you have half the butter. A croissant uses 80g and leaves $2.40 after costs. A butter cookie uses 20g and leaves $1.00.
Per kilo of butter, that's $30 from croissants and $50 from cookies.

options.text: All butter to croissants. They earn the most per item
options.feedback: Per item, yes. But butter is what's scarce now, and every kilo spent this way gives up $20 you could have earned with cookies.

options.text: Shift more butter to cookies, but keep a smaller daily croissant batch for regulars
options.feedback: You earn more from each kilo and keep the item people come in for. The question shifts from "what earns most per item" to "what earns most per kilo."

options.text: Cut every butter item by the same amount
options.feedback: Simple and fair across the menu, but it ignores which products make the best use of the butter you have.

cards.softwareNote: A software product can run short too, for example of server capacity for a heavy AI feature. The same question applies: which customers and uses earn the most per unit of the scarce resource?

cards.title: Who gets the 100 croissants?
body: Say you chose B again. You bake 100 croissants a day. On day two, an office manager buys 40 at 7:05 a.m. Regulars arriving at 8 find an empty tray.

options.text: Stay first-come, first-served with no limit
options.feedback: Easy to run, but it rewards whoever arrives first with the biggest order. The line gets longer and regulars stop coming.

options.text: Open online preorders the night before, limit four per person, keep 30 for walk-ins
options.feedback: The limit removes the reason to bulk-buy, and preorders end the dawn line. Walk-ins still have a chance.

options.text: Reserve them all for members of your loyalty app
options.feedback: Regulars feel rewarded, but new customers, your future regulars, never get to try one.

cards.title: Six weeks later, the butter is back.
body: Say you chose B. Deliveries and butter prices return to normal. Croissants still sell well at $4.25. What now?

options.text: Keep $4.25. Customers have shown they'll pay it
options.feedback: You earn $0.25 more per croissant, but you break the promise on your sign. The next time you explain a price rise, fewer people will believe you.

options.text: Go back to $4 as promised, and keep preorders if customers liked them
options.feedback: You give up a little margin and earn trust you can draw on in the next shortage. The useful parts of the crisis plan stay.

options.text: Drop to $3.50 for a month to celebrate
options.feedback: A nice gesture that brings people back, but it can reset what customers think a croissant should cost.

cards.title: Shortage pricing has limits.
body: This bakery sells a treat. For essentials like water, fuel or medicine after a disaster, even cost-based raises can look like exploitation. Many places also have rules on prices during declared emergencies, so check local rules first.
And a shortage only explains a price while it lasts. Tie every temporary change to a clear end, or customers will set the end date for you.

cards.title: A shortage is four decisions, not one price.
body: Each choice used an idea from this unit:
list: **Price → Supply and demand:** less supply pushes prices up, but the reason for a rise shapes how fair it feels
**Butter → Opportunity cost:** each kilo used one way can't be used another
**Customers → Incentives:** limits and preorders change how people behave
**After → Scarcity:** the higher price was tied to the shortage, so it ends with it
cards.callout: **Try it today:** name the input your business could run short of. Write down which product earns the most per unit of it.
